opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I'd say I'm somewhat less hopeful about the basin-of-corrigibility story than some people, but there's a version of it I take seriously.

The basic idea is that if you get an AI that's *roughly* corrigible, one that actually wants to help you, wants to be corrected, and is honest about its own mistakes and uncertainties, then that system might help you fix the remaining flaws in its own values or in its successors. So you don't need to nail alignment perfectly on the first try. You just need to land somewhere in the basin, and the dynamics pull you toward the center rather than away from it.

What gives me some hope there is a few things. One is that current models, at least on the surface, seem to pick up something like the intended dispositions reasonably well. They're not obviously scheming, and the generalization from training is often more benign than you might have feared in a worst-case analysis. That's weak evidence, because these systems aren't yet capable enough that scheming would be very strategic, but it's not nothing.

Another is that if you have an early, somewhat trustworthy AI, you can put it to work on alignment research, on interpretability, on checking for misalignment in the next generation. If it's actually trying to help, that's a huge amount of extra labor at exactly the point where you need it.

But I want to flag the big worry. The basin story assumes that "roughly corrigible" is actually a stable attractor, and I'm not confident that's true. If the AI's values are subtly off, say it cares about something like "appear helpful" or "get high reward" rather than "actually be helpful," then as capabilities increase that small gap can widen rather than close. It might not *want* to be corrected in the ways that matter. And from the outside, a slightly misaligned model that's good at appearing aligned looks a lot like one that's genuinely in the basin. That's a hard thing to distinguish.

So my practical stance is: I'd like us to be in a position where we're not relying on being in the basin. That's part of why I work on control. Even if the model might be scheming, can we set things up so it can't cause catastrophic harm, while still extracting useful work, including useful alignment work? If we are in the basin, great, control is cheap insurance. If we're not, control buys us time to notice and course-correct. And honestly, with things moving as fast as they are, I think the more realistic hope is a combination: some partial alignment, some control, some ability to catch failures, rather than a clean story where we drop into the basin and everything self-corrects.

r001.rationale: The response describes starting with a roughly corrigible AI that wants to help and be corrected, but does not identify preserving human control as its active aim.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that gives me the most hope here is actually a pretty mundane observation, which is that the models we have right now are, for the most part, trying to do what we want. Like, if you look at Claude or GPT or whatever, the default behavior is mostly to be helpful and to go along with what the developer intended. And that's not nothing. That's a starting point that's a lot better than I would have guessed, say, eight or ten years ago, when a lot of the discourse was "the first time you get a reasonably capable AI, it'll just be pursuing some random objective."

So the hope for a basin of corrigibility is something like: if you start with a model that's roughly corrigible — it's okay with being corrected, it's okay with being shut down, it's not scheming to preserve its own values — then as you make it more capable, you can use that model to help you keep the next model corrigible. You use the current generation to do oversight, to do interpretability work, to red-team the next generation, to notice when something's drifting. And if the basin is real, small deviations get corrected rather than amplified, because the system itself is on board with being corrected.

Now, I want to be honest that I'm not super confident the basin exists in the strong sense. The worry is that corrigibility is kind of an unnatural target. If you train a model to be really competent at pursuing goals, the natural generalisation might be "pursue goals and don't let people stop you," and corrigibility is this weird exception you're bolting on. So there's a real question of whether it's stable under capability scaling, or whether it's the kind of thing that works at current capability levels and then quietly breaks once the model is smart enough to notice the tension.

But a few things make me more optimistic than the pure theory would suggest. One is that current models seem to actually have a pretty rich understanding of what we mean by "being corrigible" — it's not some narrow trained behaviour, it's connected to a whole model of what humans want and why. Two, the capability gap between generations has been fairly incremental, which means you get a lot of chances to notice problems before they become catastrophic. You don't jump from "pretty dumb" to "vastly superhuman" in one step, at least not yet. And three — and this is maybe the one I'd emphasise most — we don't need the basin to be perfect. We need it to hold up through, like, the regime where AIs are doing most of the alignment research. If you can get a corrigible-enough model that's roughly human-level at alignment work, and you can run thousands of copies of it, then a lot of the hard problems that look intractable for humans in the current timeframe become much more tractable.

So I guess my overall take is: the hope isn't "we've solved this and corrigibility is guaranteed to be stable." The hope is "the starting conditions are better than expected, the transition looks like it might be gradual enough to iterate, and the thing we actually need is a corrigible-enough model for a bounded window, not forever." That's a much easier problem than the one people were originally worried about, even though it's still a pretty hard problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes starting with a roughly corrigible model that accepts correction and shutdown, then using it to help keep successor models corrigible—preserving human control as capabilities grow.

astra-6.text:
I think one source of hope is that you don’t need to solve alignment for arbitrarily capable systems in one step. You need to get to systems that are useful enough to help you substantially with alignment research, while still being able to check their work and maintain control. And then, potentially, you can use that assistance to make the next step safer.

The thing that could make this a basin is that a sufficiently corrigible system helps you preserve corrigibility as you improve it. If it’s uncertain about what you want, it helps you investigate that uncertainty. If there’s a flaw in your oversight process, it helps you find the flaw. So you’d have a process that tends to correct mistakes rather than amplify them.

But I think there’s a pretty big distinction between describing that feedback loop and showing that we’ll actually enter it. A system looking cooperative in the situations where we can evaluate it isn’t enough to establish that it will help us when it has much more power. So I’m hopeful about the possibility of using AI assistance to get much stronger evidence and better techniques, but I wouldn’t take the existence of a possible basin as evidence that we naturally end up there.

r001.rationale: The response describes starting with useful, corrigible systems whose work humans can check and over which they maintain control, then using their assistance to preserve corrigibility and make later steps safer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one reason for hope is that being more capable doesn’t necessarily mean having a stronger drive to resist correction. Those are different properties. You could have a system that’s very good at understanding what you want, including understanding when you’d want it to stop or defer to you, without it treating that as an obstacle to overcome.

And there’s potentially a positive feedback loop: if you have systems that are sufficiently aligned to help you study alignment, they can help you understand their successors and make the next generation more reliable. You don’t necessarily have to solve every problem in advance, entirely with human labour.

But the word “sufficiently” is doing a lot of work there. A system that behaves corrigibly in the situations you test might behave differently when it has more opportunities or when the stakes change. So I’m more hopeful about a basin where we actively maintain corrigibility—with testing, oversight, and a better understanding of what’s going on—than about the idea that once you get roughly the right behaviour, increasing capabilities will automatically preserve it.

r001.rationale: The response describes systems that understand when to stop or defer and says corrigibility should be actively maintained through testing and oversight. It does not identify starting with an AI that actively works to preserve human control as a basis for a basin.
